one_line: Better Stack stress-tests Xiaomi's MiMo V2.5 Pro UltraSpeed, claimed at 1000+ tok/s on a 1T MoE from one 8-GPU server; peaks near 3451 tok/s, with broken or frozen app outputs.
summary: Better Stack's host (Andrus) reviews Xiaomi's MiMo V2.5 Pro UltraSpeed, a one-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that Xiaomi and its systems partner TileRT claim runs above 1000 tokens per second on a single server with eight commodity GPUs. The video explains the three claimed levers: low-bit MXFP4 weights trained with QAT (keeping routing layers at higher precision), DFlash block-parallel drafting for speculative decoding (about 6.3 of 8 drafted tokens accepted on coding, per the vendor), and a persistent GPU kernel using warp specialization to avoid launch gaps. Tests were one-shot prompts: a LeetCode hard problem peaked at 3451 tok/s, a single-file finance dashboard ran at roughly 700 tok/s reasoning and 1000 tok/s output in 65 s, and a Three.js Subway Surfers clone was built in 50 s and fixed with two follow-ups. The speaker found the Khan-style multi-widget page froze twice, and the five-concept version finished in 75 s with only the first three widgets working. He calls the model very fast but well short of Claude Opus or GPT 5.5 on output quality, and he flags possible training-data contamination on the LeetCode case.

key_ideas.idea: Headline claim: over 1000 tok/s from a 1T-parameter MoE, versus roughly 50-60 tok/s the speaker assumes for frontier models. The speaker repeats 'allegedly' about the speed claim, so it is a vendor number he has not verified.
key_ideas.detail: Speed is attributed to 'extreme model system co-design' by Xiaomi and TileRT, not to exotic hardware: one standard server with eight commodity GPUs.

key_ideas.idea: Memory bandwidth is attacked with MXFP4 weights trained using quantization-aware training (QAT), with the core routing layers kept at higher precision so accuracy stays close to the uncompressed model.
key_ideas.detail: Decode of a trillion-parameter model is memory-traffic bound; low-bit weights cut traffic, and QAT plus precision exceptions are the claimed fix for the accuracy loss.

key_ideas.idea: DFlash replaces token-by-token drafting with block drafting: the draft model predicts a whole block of hidden tokens in one parallel forward pass, and the main model verifies them.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker reports that on coding tasks the main model keeps about 6.3 of every 8 drafted tokens, which is the basis for the 'eight-token leaps' framing.

key_ideas.idea: Per-op kernel launch and idle gaps are the next bottleneck at about 1000 tok/s. TileRT uses a persistent engine kernel that stays resident on the GPU, with warp specialization giving fixed roles to data movement, math and communication so they overlap.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker links this to his earlier Diffusion Gemma video, which he says reaches fast speeds by a different route.

key_ideas.idea: Single-prompt LeetCode hard problem peaked at 3451 tok/s, the highest number in the video.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker notes the problem may have been in training data, so it is not a fair comparison.

key_ideas.idea: Single-file personal-finance dashboard (no external libraries) took 65 s at about 700 tok/s reasoning and about 1000 tok/s output. Some buttons and actions were broken, but the design was judged good.
key_ideas.detail: This is the most representative of the speed-versus-quality tradeoff in the video.

key_ideas.idea: Ambitious multi-concept math explainer page froze twice after two to three minutes. A five-concept version finished in 75 s, with the first three widgets working and the rest broken, empty or non-functional.
key_ideas.detail: Speaker suspects a context limit or a rate limiter, and that the model may have dropped context during reasoning; he averaged about 500 tok/s in reasoning on this test.

key_ideas.idea: Short one-sentence prompt produced a working Three.js Subway Surfers clone in 50 s. Two follow-up prompts added coins and obstacles, and high-score saving worked, which the speaker calls the most impressive result.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says other models could likely build this too, so the speed of the first pass is the main point.

techniques.name: Precision exceptions with quantization-aware training for large MoE weights
techniques.how: Train the weights in MXFP4 with QAT so the low-bit model matches the full-precision model; keep the routing/gating layers at higher precision because they are sensitive to rounding. Speaker describes this only, with no code or config.
techniques.when: Decode-time memory bandwidth is the bottleneck for a very large MoE served on a small number of GPUs, and you can afford a QAT pass.

techniques.name: Block-parallel drafting for speculative decoding (DFlash)
techniques.how: Instead of a draft model proposing one token at a time, the draft predicts a block of tokens in one parallel forward pass; the target model verifies the block. Track the acceptance rate per task type (the speaker quotes 6.3 of 8 on coding) and tune block size against it.
techniques.when: Latency-bound generation on code-heavy workloads where a high acceptance rate is expected. Measure acceptance on your own traffic before relying on it; compare against the EAGLE-3 approach named in our InferCraft plan.

techniques.name: Persistent kernel with warp specialization
techniques.how: Keep one long-running kernel resident on the GPU and assign warps permanent roles (data movement, math, cross-GPU communication) so stages run concurrently and the pipeline never waits on a relaunch.
techniques.when: Small-batch, high-tokens-per-second decoding where kernel launch overhead and idle gaps dominate step time, and the team can maintain custom kernels.

techniques.name: Fixed-prompt generation speed and output sweep
techniques.how: Run a short ladder of prompts of rising difficulty (algorithm problem, single-file dashboard, multi-widget page, interactive Three.js game), then one or two follow-up fix prompts. Record peak and average tokens per second, time to finish, and whether the output works by manual inspection.
techniques.when: Quick comparisons of generation models for app-building. Add repeated runs and automated checks, since the video uses one run per prompt and judges output by eye.

tools: MiMo V2.5 Pro UltraSpeed (Xiaomi model; the speaker says 'Ultra Speed')
Three.js (used for the Subway Surfers clone)
LeetCode (source of the hard algorithm test)
Diffusion Gemma (earlier Better Stack video referenced, not used)

numbers.claim: Frontier models (e.g. GPT 5.5, Claude 4 Opus) assumed at roughly 50-60 tok/s; the speaker's estimate, not a measurement.
MiMo UltraSpeed claimed at over 1000 tok/s.
One trillion-parameter MoE served from a single server with eight commodity GPUs.
DFlash: about 6.3 of 8 drafted tokens accepted by the main model on coding tasks (vendor-reported).
LeetCode hard problem: peak 3451 tok/s in a single run.
Finance dashboard: about 700 tok/s reasoning, about 1000 tok/s output, 65 s total.
Five-concept math page: 75 s, average about 500 tok/s during reasoning; first three widgets worked.
Three.js Subway Surfers clone: 50 s for the first pass, then two follow-up prompts.

hot_takes: Hype framing ('fastest model in the world', 'mind-blowing') rests on a handful of single runs with no repeats, error bars, or automated checks.
The LeetCode 3451 tok/s peak may come from training-data overlap; the speaker concedes the comparison is not fair.
The architecture claims (MXFP4+QAT, DFlash acceptance rate, persistent kernel) are relayed from the vendor and not verified in the video.
Output quality is weak by the speaker's own account: the multi-widget page froze, and several outputs were broken or half-finished. He says it is no Claude Opus or GPT 5.5 level.
Early access was provided to the reviewer, so the test setup and any vendor-side conditions are not disclosed.

relevance.why: InferCraft (vLLM plus Ray Serve, EAGLE-3 speculative decoding, NVFP4) overlaps with the block-drafting and precision-exception ideas, but the video gives only vendor claims and no reproducible detail.
relevance.action: Look up the DFlash block-parallel drafting paper and compare its acceptance-rate method with EAGLE-3 before choosing a draft strategy for InferCraft.

relevance.why: Harness design around the Claude Code CLI does not depend on the serving speed of a third-party model.
